sentences.text: Istiodactylus was a large pterosaur with a wingspan estimated between 4.3 and 5 meters.
Its skull measured approximately 45 centimeters in length and appeared relatively short and broad compared to other flying reptiles.
The snout was low and blunt, containing a semicircular row of 48 teeth.
Some estimates suggest the skull could reach 56 centimeters, while the wingspan might have approached five meters, roughly half the size of the largest Pteranodon specimens.
Because of its rounded and flattened beak shape, this animal is sometimes referred to as the duck-billed pterosaur.
Isolated wing-bone fragments indicate that certain individuals may have achieved a wingspan of 8 meters.
The sharp, leaf-shaped teeth were laterally compressed to act as an adaptation for cutting meat and were closely interlocked at the front of the jaws.
The first fossil remains were discovered on the Isle of Wight, England, in 1887.
In that same year, Harry Govier Seeley named fossil pelvis remains from the site as Ornithodesmus cluniculus, believing them to belong to a bird.
The genus Istiodactylus was formally described by Howse, Milner, and Martill in 2001.
By 1901, a specific specimen had become the holotype for the new species O. latidens.
Reginald W. Hooley later described two additional specimens of O. latidens in 1913.
Researchers suggest that Istiodactylus was a scavenger that used its teeth to cut morsels from large carcasses like a cookie cutter.
It is hypothesized that the wings were adapted for soaring to locate carcasses before terrestrial carnivores arrived.
The fact that istiodactylid fossils are found in freshwater or brackish water deposits with terrestrial input supports the idea that they scavenged in terrestrial settings.
Witton found that the feet of istiodactylids were too small relative to their body size to be used for climbing or suspension.
Unlike ducks, Istiodactylus had small sharp teeth and may have eaten fish or scavenged carrion.
A 2012 study proposed that Istiodactylus was primarily a scavenger.
Istiodactylus belongs to the family Istiodactylidae.
The genus authority for Istiodactylus is Howse, Milner, & Martill, 2001.
In 2001, Howse et al. established the family Istiodactylidae for Istiodactylus.
In 1913, Hooley classified Istiodactylus latidens as most similar to Scaphognathus and Dimorphodon, considering it a modified form of Scaphognathus.
In 2003, both David Unwin and Alexander W. Kellner classified Istiodactylus within Ornithocheiroidea, though the specific grouping varied between their studies.
Istiodactylus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 120 million years ago.
Istiodactylus fossils are found in the Wessex and Vectis Formations, representing river and coastal environments.
All known remains of istiodactylids date from the Barremian to Aptian ages of the Early Cretaceous period and are found in the Northern Hemisphere.
The time range for Istiodactylus is from the Barremian to the Aptian, between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago.
Samuel W. Williston disagreed with some of Reginald W. Hooley's conclusions regarding the anatomy and classification of the animal.
In 1993, researchers concluded that the holotype specimen of Ornithodesmus cluniculus belonged to a maniraptoran dinosaur rather than a pterosaur.
In 2006, Lü and colleagues concluded that I. sinensis was a junior synonym of Nurhachius ignaciobritoi.
The interrelationships and exact content of the family Istiodactylidae remain unclear and require reappraisal due to rapid discoveries in the 21st century.
In 2010, Attila Ősi agreed that Istiodactylus could cut meat but noted it could not process food with precisely occluding teeth.
In 2006, Lü Jun-Chang et al. concluded that I. sinensis is a junior synonym of the istiodactylid Nurhachius.
